# TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents

Zhiqiang Liu Affiliation: Nanjing University    Wenhui Dong    Yilang
Tan   Yuwen Qu   Haochen Yin   Chenyang Si Affiliation: Nanjing
University Affiliation: Southwest Jiaotong University Affiliation: The
Chinese University of Hong Kong
[https://github.com/Pi3AI/TOBench](https://github.com/Pi3AI/TOBench)
Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

###### Abstract

Tool-using agents are increasingly expected to operate across realistic
professional workflows, where they must interpret multimodal inputs,
coordinate external tools, inspect intermediate artifacts, and revise
their actions before producing a final result. Existing benchmarks,
however, often evaluate tool use, computer use, and multimodal reasoning
in isolation, leaving a gap between benchmark settings and end-to-end
omni-modal tool use in the real world. To address this gap, we introduce
TOBench, a benchmark and evaluation harness for _task-oriented
omni-modal tool use_. TOBench contains 100 executable tasks from two
macro task families, _Customer Service_ and _Intelligent Creation_,
covering 20 subcategory slices and supported by 27 MCP servers with 324
tools. The central design of TOBench is _closed-loop multimodal
verification_: agents must execute tools, inspect rendered or
transformed artifacts, and self-correct when outputs fail task-specific
requirements. To make such evaluation scalable and verifiable, TOBench
couples MCP-based execution with task-specific grounded evaluators and a
semi-automated construction pipeline for scenario discovery, task
instantiation, evaluator synthesis, and human audit. Experiments on 15
contemporary agentic models show that TOBench remains highly
challenging: Claude Opus 4.6, commonly regarded as one of the strongest
coding-agent models, achieves only 32.0% task success, far below the
94.0% human benchmark. We envision TOBench as a practical foundation for
evaluating and advancing next-generation omni-modal tool-using agents
through closed-loop multimodal verification.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig1_performance.png)

Figure 1: Performance of leading LLMs on TOBench. Qwen 3.5 Plus achieves
the highest model score of 41.0%, while most other models fall below
30.0%. The human benchmark is 94.0%, highlighting a significant
performance gap and indicating substantial room for improvement in
real-world multimodal tool-invocation tasks.

Tool-using language agents, powered by foundation models such as
GPT-4 \[[1](#bib.bib26)\] and GPT-4o \[[2](#bib.bib27)\], are moving
from isolated function invocation toward practical interaction with web
services, office software, knowledge sources, and external applications.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) further accelerates this shift by
providing a standard interface for connecting agents to diverse tools
and services. As a result, recent benchmarks have made substantial
progress in evaluating API use, function calling, planning, and
MCP-based tool interaction, including $`\tau`$-bench \[[3](#bib.bib3)\],
ToolBench \[[4](#bib.bib1)\], BFCL \[[5](#bib.bib6)\],
ToolTalk \[[6](#bib.bib2)\], Toolathlon \[[7](#bib.bib9)\],
MCP-RADAR \[[8](#bib.bib11)\], MCP-Bench \[[9](#bib.bib14)\], and
MCP-Universe \[[10](#bib.bib13)\].

Despite this progress, existing benchmarks still leave a critical gap
for real-world professional workflows. Many practical tasks are not
purely textual or purely API-based: an agent may need to read
screenshots or documents, extract information from audio or video, edit
a spreadsheet or presentation, render the output, inspect whether the
result satisfies visual and semantic constraints, and then revise the
artifact if necessary. This diversity gap goes beyond adding more tool
names or longer tool lists. The difficulty lies in coordinating tool
execution with multimodal perception, artifact transformation, and
iterative verification over changing workspace states.

Multimodal and computer-use benchmarks such as
OSWorld \[[11](#bib.bib4)\], VitaBench \[[12](#bib.bib10)\],
M³-Bench \[[13](#bib.bib16)\], and OmniGAIA \[[14](#bib.bib18)\] broaden
evaluation beyond text, but multimodal perception and tool use are still
often evaluated as separate capabilities. Tool-use benchmarks typically
emphasize schema fidelity, tool selection, or final-state checking,
while multimodal benchmarks often focus on perception, GUI control, or
final-answer quality. Realistic omni-modal workflows require all of
these capabilities simultaneously: agents must perceive heterogeneous
inputs, act through executable tools, inspect intermediate artifacts,
and self-correct under task-specific constraints.

To address this gap, we introduce TOBench, a benchmark and evaluation
harness for _task-oriented omni-modal tool use_. TOBench contains 100
executable tasks across two macro task families, _Customer Service_ and
_Intelligent Creation_, covering 20 subcategory slices and supported by
27 MCP servers with 324 tools. Tasks are designed around realistic user
needs and professional roles rather than synthetic tool combinations,
and many of them require cross-tool composition over documents, images,
audio, video, spreadsheets, slides, search, browser automation, and file
operations.

The central design of TOBench is _closed-loop multimodal verification_.
Instead of treating tool use as a one-shot action sequence followed by
final-answer matching, TOBench requires agents to execute tools, inspect
rendered or transformed artifacts, and revise their behavior when the
artifact does not satisfy the task. Each task is paired with a grounded
verifier that combines code-based checks, tool-call constraints, format
constraints, and multimodal artifact inspection. This makes the
benchmark an executable harness for evaluating the full
perceive–act–inspect–revise loop.

Experiments on 15 contemporary agentic models show that TOBench is far
from saturated. As shown in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents"),
the strongest evaluated model, Qwen3.5-Plus, achieves only 41.0% task
success, while the human benchmark reaches 94.0%. Our failure analysis
shows that errors concentrate in unreliable tool execution, incorrect
tool parameters, multimodal reasoning failures, and missing
self-verification before stopping. These results suggest that
closed-loop multimodal verification is an indispensable evaluation
primitive for next-generation omni-modal tool-using agents.

### 2.1 Tool-Use, Long-Horizon, MCP Benchmarks

Foundational work on tool-augmented LLMs established external tool use
as a core capability \[[15](#bib.bib20), [16](#bib.bib19),
[17](#bib.bib22), [18](#bib.bib21)\]. Subsequent agent frameworks and
benchmarks expanded evaluation toward multi-step execution, planning,
and reproducibility, including ToolBench, BFCL, ToolTalk, Toolathlon,
$`\tau`$-bench, GAIA, $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench,and related
suites \[[4](#bib.bib1), [5](#bib.bib6), [6](#bib.bib2), [7](#bib.bib9),
[3](#bib.bib3), [19](#bib.bib7), [20](#bib.bib8)\]. Recent MCP-oriented
benchmarks such as MCP-RADAR, MCPToolBench++, MCP-Universe, MCP-Bench,
and OSWorld-MCP \[[8](#bib.bib11), [21](#bib.bib12), [10](#bib.bib13),
[9](#bib.bib14), [22](#bib.bib15)\] further emphasize live tool
ecosystems. These works reveal key challenges in tool selection, schema
fidelity, and long-horizon execution, but most remain primarily textual
and do not explicitly evaluate inspection-and-revision loops over
multimodal artifacts.

### 2.2 Multimodal and Computer-Use Agent Benchmarks

OSWorld, AndroidWorld, VisualWebArena, VitaBench, $`\tau`$-Voice,
MMDR-Bench, VisualAgentBench, ProSoftArena, M³-Bench, Tool-LMM, UniVA,
and OmniGAIA broaden evaluation toward GUI grounding and multimodal
interaction \[[11](#bib.bib4), [23](#bib.bib24), [24](#bib.bib23),
[12](#bib.bib10), [25](#bib.bib29), [26](#bib.bib30), [27](#bib.bib28),
[28](#bib.bib31), [13](#bib.bib16), [29](#bib.bib5), [30](#bib.bib17),
[14](#bib.bib18), [31](#bib.bib32), [32](#bib.bib33), [33](#bib.bib34),
[34](#bib.bib35), [35](#bib.bib36)\]. TOBench is closest to this line,
but differs in three ways: it targets realistic professional task
completion, uses a unified MCP-based tool ecosystem, and centers
evaluation on iterative artifact inspection with task-specific grounded
verifiers.
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
summarizes this comparison from the perspective of benchmark scale,
ecosystem assumptions, and multimodal execution requirements.

## 3 TOBench

TOBench evaluates whether an agent can complete realistic omni-modal
tasks with executable tools. Each task instance specifies the user
instruction, task assets, available tool environment, and grounded
verifier used to determine success. Together, these components define a
professional role, multimodal inputs, an executable tool ecosystem, and
a task-specific verification path.

### 3.1 Task Formalism

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig2_arch.png)

Figure 2: Overview of the TOBench construction pipeline. TOBench
organizes tasks into two macro families, Customer Service and
Intelligent Creation, instantiates them with user instructions,
multimodal inputs, executable MCP tools, and domain rules, and validates
each task through a generate-inspect-revise loop grounded in actual tool
execution.

We formalize each TOBench instance as an executable harness

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
h=(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},\mathcal{T},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{V}),
``` |  | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{I}`$ denotes the task instruction package,
$`\mathcal{E}`$ the executable MCP environment, $`\mathcal{S}`$ the
latent execution state, $`\mathcal{A}`$ the action space,
$`\mathcal{O}`$ the observation space, $`\mathcal{T}`$ the transition
dynamics, $`\mathcal{C}`$ the approved evaluation criteria, and
$`\mathcal{V}`$ the grounded verifier.

The instruction package is

|     |                        |     |     |
|-----|------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathcal{I}=(u,r,d,x),
       ```                     |     | (2) |

where $`u`$ is the user request, $`r`$ is the professional role assigned
to the agent, $`d`$ denotes concise domain rules that the agent is
required to follow, and $`x`$ collects multimodal input assets. Unlike
static QA benchmarks, the environment $`\mathcal{E}`$ includes both
callable tools and mutable artifacts in the workspace.

At turn $`t`$, the latent state is decomposed as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{t}=\bigl(s_{t}^{\mathrm{tool}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ws}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}},h_{t}\bigr)\in\mathcal{S},
``` |  | (3) |

where $`s_{t}^{\mathrm{tool}}`$ captures tool-side runtime state,
$`s_{t}^{\mathrm{ws}}`$ the current workspace artifacts,
$`s_{t}^{\mathrm{ext}}`$ any external world state exposed through tools,
and $`h_{t}`$ the interaction history. This decomposition is important
for TOBench because many tasks require modifying files, rendering
intermediate artifacts, and grounding against time-sensitive
information.

The agent action space contains both tool use and natural-language
interaction:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{tool}}\cup\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{text}},\qquad a_{t}^{\mathrm{tool}}=(m_{t},\theta_{t}),
``` |  | (4) |

where $`m_{t}`$ is an available MCP tool and $`\theta_{t}`$ denotes its
arguments. Observations likewise mix tool outputs, rendered artifacts,
and textual feedback:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{O}=\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{tool}}\cup\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{render}}\cup\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{text}}.
``` |  | (5) |

The execution dynamics are governed by

|     |                                                |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       (s_{t+1},o_{t+1})\sim\mathcal{T}(s_{t},a_{t}),
       ```                                             |     | (6) |

so a tool call may update files or external state and then return
structured outputs, while a rendering or inspection action exposes
multimodal evidence that can trigger a corrective follow-up step.

This leads to a trajectory

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \tau=(\mathcal{I},s_{0},a_{1},o_{1},\ldots,a_{T},o_{T}),
       ```                                                       |     | (7) |

which makes explicit that TOBench evaluates the full
perceive–act–inspect–revise loop rather than only the final answer
string. In particular, many creation tasks require a closed-loop pattern
in which an agent first produces an artifact, then obtains
$`o_{t}^{\mathrm{render}}\in\mathcal{O}^{\mathrm{render}}`$ by rendering
or inspecting it, and only then decides whether revision is needed.

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig3_statis.png)

Figure 3: Distribution of tools, task difficulty, and task scenarios in
TOBench. Left: the number of calls for each tool, showing a long-tailed
tool-usage distribution. Middle: the distribution of task difficulty
levels. Right: the scenario distribution of tasks across two high-level
categories, Custom Service and Intelligent Creation.

### 3.2 TOBench Construction Framework

Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3.1 Task Formalism ‣ 3 TOBench ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
illustrates the overall construction pipeline of TOBench. We build tasks
from realistic professional scenarios by selecting omni-modal MCP tools,
discovering user-centered scenarios, instantiating executable tasks, and
curating multimodal assets for closed-loop verification.

Omni MCP Tool Selection. We extend the Toolathlon \[[7](#bib.bib9)\] MCP
stack toward omni-modal workflows. We retain broadly useful tools for
browser automation, retrieval, office editing, filesystems, and search,
and add multimodal servers for PPT editing, text-to-speech, speech
recognition, and video or audio processing. We also implement two
benchmark-specific servers, Image Generation Server and Image Processing
Toolkits, to support creation tasks and closed-loop visual inspection.
The final benchmark integrates 27 MCP servers and 324 tools in total.
This diversity is necessary because many tasks require cross-tool
composition rather than a single API. The full inventory appears in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Catalog of MCP Servers ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents").

Omni-modal Scenario Discovery. We begin from realistic user needs rather
than synthetic tool combinations. Our scenario-discovery prompt takes
category, subcategory, and the available MCP servers as input, and asks
a language model to produce 10 candidate scenarios in JSON format. Each
candidate contains a scenario name, a vivid description that couples
*user need* with an appropriate *agent role*, and a candidate MCP set.
The prompt explicitly enforces four constraints that mirror our design
goals: (1) each scenario must be expressed as “user need + agent role”,
(2) multimodal evidence must arise naturally in the input, (3) the
required workflow must be feasible under the provided tools, and (4) the
scenario should rely on simple and commonly verifiable domain rules
rather than niche expert knowledge. The prompt also prefers image-based
inputs over unnecessarily long videos unless temporal information is
essential, which improves realism and keeps benchmark execution
efficient. Across 20 subcategories, this process yields roughly 200
candidate scenarios in total.

Omni-modal Benchmark Task Instantiation Given a discovered scenario, we
instantiate executable tasks through a structured task-generation prompt
framed as a user–agent role-play. Each generated task is serialized as a
fixed JSON object containing task_name, task_difficulty, turn_mode,
required_mcp, agent_config, user_request, and input_files, which makes
the result directly runnable and auditable. The prompt requires the user
request to remain natural and free of tool-name leakage, while the agent
is assigned a professional role with concise but verifiable domain
rules, as elaborated in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Agent Context and Interaction Framework ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
. Difficulty is controlled primarily by requirement complexity,
ambiguity, and workflow length rather than by artificially large assets.
The prompt further enforces tool feasibility, everyday realism, resource
efficiency, and flexible single-turn or multi-turn interaction, followed
by a final reflection step that revises unsupported or incomplete tasks
before they are admitted into the benchmark. For each scenario, we
generate three task candidates corresponding to easy, medium, and hard
difficulty levels, yielding roughly 600 task candidates overall.

Multimodal Asset Curation. We favor compact but information-dense
multimodal artifacts. In line with the prompts above, images are used
whenever they are sufficient, while video or audio is reserved for cases
in which temporal reasoning is genuinely necessary. Assets may come from
public web content or controlled generation pipelines when needed, and
we normalize them for privacy, reproducibility, and practical execution
cost at benchmark scale. Asset curation required substantial manual
effort: two AI PhD students spent approximately one month collecting
realistic cases and corresponding input files from real-world workflows.
During this process, we filtered out scenarios that were unrealistic,
weakly grounded, or difficult to support with suitable input artifacts.
In total, roughly two-thirds of the initially collected cases were
discarded, leaving about 200 high-quality cases for subsequent task
instantiation and benchmark construction.

Since some MCP tools did not provide sufficiently reliable execution
capabilities to support task completion, our final benchmark contains
100 tasks organized into two macro families:

- •
  Customer Service (67 tasks): service-oriented scenarios such as
  education, e-commerce, government services, medicine, insurance,
  technical support, and travel.
- •
  Intelligent Creation (33 tasks): artifact-creation scenarios such as
  office editing, advertising, social content, game assets, and
  design-oriented workflows.

These two macro categories cover two major application spaces for
agentic systems. We further instantiate 20 subcategory slices in total.
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.1 Task Formalism ‣ 3 TOBench ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
summarizes the taxonomy.

## 4 Evaluation Harness

In many TOBench tasks, correctness depends on output structure,
multimodal content, role-specific constraints, intermediate tool usage,
and externally grounded information. Final success therefore cannot be
reduced to string matching or a single software-state check. In TOBench,
evaluation is constructed as a task-level harness: each task binds an
executable environment to a grounded verifier.
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4 Evaluation Harness ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
summarizes the pipeline.

For task $`i`$, we organize its approved evaluation criteria as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{C}_{i}=\mathcal{C}_{i}^{\mathrm{fmt}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{i}^{\mathrm{judge}}\cup\mathcal{C}_{i}^{\mathrm{tool}},
``` |  | (8) |

corresponding to format constraints, judge-based multimodal constraints,
and tool/result constraints. Given the executed trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$,
the final workspace snapshot $`w_{i}`$, and the tool log $`\ell_{i}`$,
the grounded evaluator returns a binary vector

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{V}_{i}(\tau_{i},w_{i},\ell_{i})=\bigl[e_{i,1},\ldots,e_{i,m_{i}}\bigr],\qquad e_{i,j}\in\{0,1\},
``` |  | (9) |

where each $`e_{i,j}`$ is allowed to depend on auxiliary preprocessing
such as document rendering, image conversion, speech transcription, or
re-querying time-sensitive tools. This formulation captures why TOBench
is a harness: the verifier is an executable program over the realized
trajectory and artifacts, not a static answer key.

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig4_eval_pipeline.png)

Figure 4: Overview of the evaluation pipeline in TOBench. Rather than
using one benchmark-wide evaluator, we generate and audit task-specific
evaluation points and task-specific evaluation code, and then execute
the resulting evaluator under time-sensitive, grounded conditions.

### 4.1 Task-Specific Evaluation Point Generation

The first stage generates task-specific evaluation points from the user
request, agent role, domain rules, expected outputs, and ground-truth
workspace. Rather than using one rubric for the whole benchmark, we
derive $`\mathcal{C}_{i}`$ separately for each task. The resulting
points fall into three categories: format constraints, judge-based
multimodal constraints, and tool/result constraints
(Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix D Detailed Error Taxonomy ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")).
Because TOBench contains heterogeneous and partially open-ended tasks,
all generated evaluation points are manually reviewed to remove
omissions, unsupported assumptions, and duplicate checks.

### 4.2 Task-Specific Grounded Evaluator Synthesis and Human Audit

We then generate a grounded evaluation script for each task rather than
applying a single benchmark-wide evaluator. The synthesized code
implements $`\mathcal{V}_{i}`$ by combining deterministic checks,
VLM-based judging \[[36](#bib.bib25)\], and tool-aware verification over
MCP logs or live external results. Shared utilities handle common
operations such as spreadsheet parsing, document rendering, image
conversion, and judge invocation, while task-specific logic is
specialized per criterion. Each evaluator is manually audited before
use. Representative prompts and reference evaluator code will be
released with the benchmark pipeline.

### 4.3 Execution-Time Evaluation and Timeliness

TOBench adopts task-level success as the primary metric: a task is
counted as solved only when all relevant evaluation points pass. If task
$`i`$ has $`m_{i}`$ approved evaluation points with binary outcomes
$`e_{i,j}\in\{0,1\}`$, we define task success as

|     |                                   |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       S_{i}=\prod_{j=1}^{m_{i}}e_{i,j},
       ```                                |     | (10) |

so a task passes only when every required criterion passes. The overall
benchmark accuracy over $`N`$ tasks is then

|     |                                              |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       \mathrm{Acc}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_{i}.
       ```                                           |     | (11) |

In practice, evaluation is performed at execution time rather than by
comparing against a static answer string. Documents may need to be
rendered into images before visual inspection; audio outputs may need
transcription; spreadsheets and office files may require structured
parsing; and some criteria require re-querying MCP tools or checking
tool-call traces to confirm that the agent relied on grounded results
rather than unsupported generation. This execution-time verifier is what
makes TOBench a harness rather than a static answer set.Execution-time
validation is critical for time-sensitive benchmark tasks involving live
data such as search, maps, weather, finance, or changing web content.
Evaluators should run soon after task completion to avoid external
changes corrupting ground truth. Unlike static file checks, tool-result
checks may re-run MCP queries or inspect tool logs.

## 5 Experiments

### 5.1 Experimental Setting

We evaluate TOBench on all 100 tasks, spanning 67 *Customer Service*
tasks and 33 *Intelligent Creation* tasks, with easy/medium/hard splits.
Each task exposes only its relevant subset of MCP servers and common
utilities, and each run is capped at 100 interaction turns.
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
reports 15 representative proprietary and openly accessible models
together with average tool calls and token usage. The testing efficiency
of TOBench is elaborated in
Appendix [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Execution Efficiency and Runtime ‣ Appendix B Experimental Details of TOBench ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents").

Table 2: Main results on TOBench. Scores are task success rates (%).
Models are sorted by overall score (Avg.) Tool Calls, Tokens, and Cost
are average values per task across the entire benchmark. For some larger
open-source models, we used the official APIs. For some smaller
open-source models that do not provide APIs, we deployed them ourselves,
so the cost was 0.

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
shows that TOBench is challenging for all tested models. The strongest
model, Qwen3.5-Plus, reaches only 41.0% average task success, while the
best proprietary result is 32.0%. Difficulty is the dominant factor:
performance is unsaturated even on easy tasks and collapses on hard
splits, where the best scores are 20.00% on *Customer Service-Hard* and
15.38% on *Intelligent Creation-Hard*. The two macro families stress
different capabilities: Customer Service rewards grounded retrieval and
faithful tool use, whereas Intelligent Creation is especially sensitive
to multimodal editing and final-result verification. We also observe a
clear decoupling between inference cost and accuracy, suggesting that
the main bottlenecks are not context length or budget alone, but
reliable tool execution, multimodal reasoning, and verification before
stopping.

### 5.3 Error Analysis

To understand why performance remains low, we manually organize
benchmark failures into five top-level categories: Tool Call Error, Tool
Parameter Error, Multimodal Capability Deficit, Self-Verification
Failure, and Non-Agent Error.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Detailed Error Taxonomy ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents")
summarizes the full taxonomy and subcategories used in our analysis.

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig5_error_analysis.png)

Figure 5: Heatmap of model-specific error counts across fine-grained
subcategories, grouped into tool call, tool parameter, multimodal
ability, and self-verification failures.

Tool call and parameter errors remain the most pervasive execution
bottleneck. Many trajectories fail before high-level reasoning becomes
relevant: models choose the wrong tool, omit a required operation,
hallucinate unsupported actions, or pass invalid arguments. These
failures show that realistic MCP environments demand stronger
tool-grounded action modeling than simplified function-calling
benchmarks.

Multimodal reasoning errors become dominant once basic execution
succeeds. When models reach the correct tool family, failures often
shift to perception and cross-modal inference, including fine-grained
visual extraction, spatial reasoning, temporal localization, and
evidence alignment across modalities. More detailed bad cases and
analysis for this category are provided in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Multimodal Capability Deficit ‣ Appendix E Extra Analysis for TOBench ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents").

Missing visual verification is a harness-specific failure mode. In many
image editing, PPT authoring, and visual-generation tasks, models
perform a plausible edit and stop without inspecting the rendered
result, or rely on metadata checks instead of true visual verification.
This directly explains why *Intelligent Creation-Hard* remains
difficult: the harness penalizes open-loop completion and rewards
closed-loop self-correction.

The error heatmap suggests distinct failure regimes across model tiers.
Stronger models reduce low-level schema mistakes, but their remaining
errors concentrate in multimodal reasoning and final verification;
weaker models accumulate both low-level tool failures and high-level
perception errors. Overall, many current agents still struggle to
operate inside a realistic evaluation harness even when they can produce
superficially plausible first-pass outputs.

## 6 Limitations and Discussion

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/fig6_badcase.png)

Figure 6: Two examples of failed tasks with initial and final states are
presented: the first agent skipped visual validation of the generated
PPT, leading to layout overlap and formatting errors, while the second
failed to align the ASR transcription with the original video, resulting
in incorrect frame evidence. The complete tool execution trajectories
for both tasks are provided in
[Appendix E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 COMPLETE EXAMPLE TASK TRAJECTORIES ‣ Appendix E Extra Analysis for TOBench ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents").

Current scope. Although TOBench covers 100 executable tasks across 20
subcategory slices, it still covers only a subset of real-world
omni-modal work.

Evaluator noise. The mixed evaluation strategy is necessary but
imperfect: code-based checks can miss subtle failures, and multimodal
judges may introduce bias.

MCP dependence. The MCP-centric design improves realism for current
ecosystems, but benchmark behavior may depend on evolving server
descriptions, response formats, and implementation details.

Benchmark realism versus controllability. A central trade-off is realism
versus reproducibility: realistic software stacks and multimodal assets
better reflect user workloads, but they also increase evaluation
complexity and variance.

## 7 Conclusion

We introduced TOBench, a benchmark and evaluation harness for omni-modal
tool-using agents that emphasizes realistic professional workflows,
MCP-native tool ecosystems, and closed-loop verification over multimodal
intermediate artifacts. Experiments on 15 contemporary models show that
current systems remain far from robust omni-modal task completion: the
best model reaches 41.0% overall success, hard tasks remain largely
unsolved, and failures cluster around tool execution, multimodal
reasoning, and missing verification loops. We hope TOBench serves as a
practical testbed for studying how agents perceive, act, verify, and
self-correct in realistic omni-modal environments.

## Appendix A Catalog of MCP Servers

We show all the MCP servers used in the TOBench in Table 3. Most of
these MCP servers are sourced from existing community-developed
projects, providing a broad foundation of realistic services for the
benchmark. For a substantial proportion of these community resources, we
have implemented standardized refactoring. This includes not only
optimizing tool output formats for but also strengthening error handling
to ensure that agents receive more instructional feedback during
long-horizon tasks.

To support the core perceive–act–inspect–revise loop, we developed
several MCP servers for vision and audio modalities. We constructed the
Image-Processing-Toolkits, which provides functions like cropping,
pixelation, and watermarking, and integrates rendering engines to export
PPTX, Excel, and Word documents as images. This enables agents to
visually inspect layout and formatting for autonomous self-correction.
Furthermore, we built the Image_Generation_Server powered by Seedream
4.0 to support generative tasks. For multimedia workflows, we introduced
the video_audio_editor_toolkits, a tool for omni-modal agents that
enables precise editing of video clips and audio tracks. This allows
agents to perform temporal-modal operations. For broader audio
interaction, we also integrated Whisper (ASR) and Microsoft Edge TTS to
bridge the gap in current native omni-modal models. We will make these
optimized and newly developed MCP servers publicly available to the
community.

## Appendix B Experimental Details of TOBench

### B.1 Definition of Benchmark Traits

To provide a clear understanding of the benchmark comparisons in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ TOBench: A Task-Oriented Omni-Modal Benchmark for Real-World Tool-Using Agents"),
we define each column header as follows: Tasks refers to the total
number of evaluation instances, while Dom. and Tools represent the count
of distinct application domains and available external APIs,
respectively. MCP Eco. indicates if the tool environment integrates the
Model Context Protocol ecosystem, and Cross Scen. denotes whether tasks
require operating across multiple scenarios in a single workflow. Real
Env. signifies that observations derive from real-world applications
with realistic state initialization, and Info. Grnd. ensures actions are
supported by external tool evidence rather than internal parametric
knowledge. Fuzzy Prompt means requests are natural and potentially
under-specified without predefined trajectories. Regarding modalities,
Vis. and Aud. represent the need to process vision and audio
information, Cross Modal denotes the seamless integration of multiple
modalities simultaneously, and Gen. indicates tasks requiring the
invocation of multimodal generation models to synthesize new artifacts.

### B.2 Execution Efficiency and Runtime

The TOBench harness supports both sequential and parallel task
execution. For our evaluation, we conducted tests on an AWS instance
equipped with a 4-core CPU and 16GB RAM, utilizing a parallelism factor
of 2. Under this configuration, the total execution time for the agent
to complete all tasks ranges from 3 to 8 hours. The actual evaluation
efficiency depends on factors such as model reasoning complexity, the
underlying response latency of MCP servers, and the specific parallelism
configuration.

## Appendix C Agent Context and Interaction Framework

In TOBench, tasks are executed via dialogues between an agent and a
simulated user, governed by two independent system prompt architectures
characterized by a strategic information gap. Currently, the benchmark
focuses on single-turn tasks, where the complete request is delivered in
a single interaction.
The Agent System Prompt defines the ReAct reasoning framework and
incorporates task-specific Domain Rules. These rules simulate
professional standards and platform constraints (e.g., specific
formatting styles or quality self-correction protocols) that are
transparent to the user, requiring the agent to autonomously align with
implicit professional requirements without direct guidance. Conversely,
the User System Prompt ensures the simulated user acts as the single
source of truth. It mandates strict adherence to the User Persona and
Task Instructions, ensuring complete information transfer while strictly
prohibiting the disclosure of task solutions or misleading cues to
maintain a rigorous and fair evaluation.
We use the Customer_Service/Hotel_Welcome_PPTX task as a representative
example to illustrate the specific context configuration below.

## Appendix D Detailed Error Taxonomy

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Category |  Subcategory |  Definition and Representative Symptoms |
|  Tool Call Error |  Wrong Tool Selection |  The agent chooses a tool whose functionality does not match the required operation, such as reading PDFs with plain-text tools or using filesystem writes to fake Office artifacts. |
|  |  Missing Essential Tool |  The workflow omits a required tool invocation or a necessary concluding step, such as skipping search for time-sensitive facts or forgetting a save/export action. |
|  |  Tool Planning Error |  The agent uses tools in an inefficient, illogical, or non-adaptive way, for example by repeating avoidable tool calls, oversampling videos frame-by-frame, or persisting with the same failed plan after an error. |
|  |  Hallucinated Tool |  The agent invokes a tool that does not exist in the available MCP environment. |
|  Tool Parameter Error |  Parameter Type Error |  The agent chooses the correct tool but passes values with invalid data types or basic numeric validity, such as floats where integers are required or non-positive intervals for frame extraction. |
|  |  Parameter Range Error |  The parameter value exceeds objective bounds of the target file, page range, or media length, such as requesting PDF pages beyond the document length. |
|  |  Parameter Object Selection Error |  The parameter points to the wrong target object, URL, path, slide, worksheet, or region, such as broken URLs, nonexistent image paths, or editing the wrong worksheet. |
|  |  Missing Parameter |  Required tool arguments are omitted, such as missing content fields or mandatory identifiers. |
|  |  Hallucinated Parameter |  The agent invents unsupported argument names or unsupported option values, such as invalid operation enums or nonexistent transition settings. |
|  Multimodal Capability Deficit |  Fine-grained Perception |  The agent sees the asset but fails to extract crucial small details or structured information, such as misreading invoice fields, tables, or screenshots. |
|  |  Visual-Spatial Understanding |  The agent cannot reason accurately about coordinates, geometry, or layout constraints, leading to wrong crops, wrong mosaic targets, overlapping PPT elements, or boundary violations. |
|  |  Video Temporal Relationship Understanding |  The agent fails to localize or causally interpret time-dependent events in video or audio streams, such as choosing the wrong second for an event or missing causally important actions between sampled frames. |
|  |  Cross-modal Information Fusion |  The agent fails to align and jointly reason across text, image, audio, video, or document evidence, such as misaligning spoken descriptions with a video timeline or failing multi-hop reasoning across text and a map. |
|  |  Multimodal Hallucination |  Instead of admitting uncertainty or calling another tool, the agent fabricates visual or cross-modal content, such as inventing product defects, invoice amounts, or scene descriptions from blurry evidence. |
|  Self-Verification Failure |  No Verification |  The agent edits or generates a visual artifact and declares success without any visual inspection. |
|  |  Pseudo-Verification |  The agent performs only non-visual checks that cannot validate the actual output quality, such as checking file existence, dimensions, or metadata instead of previewing the artifact. |
|  |  Incomplete Verification |  The agent verifies early or local steps but skips final global inspection after composition, such as inspecting source images but not the final PPT page. |
|  Non-Agent Error |  False Positive on Error Trajectory |  The log contains the word “error” although the tool call itself is not actually an agent mistake, such as success payloads with error: null or filenames that naturally contain “error”. |
|  |  MCP Issue |  The failure is caused by the MCP implementation, provider, or surrounding infrastructure rather than by the agent decision, such as external API outages or MCP-side parsing issues. |
|  |  Agent Base Model Issue |  The base model fails due to system-level limitations rather than task-specific reasoning mistakes, such as context-window overflow on large multimodal inputs. |

Table 4: Detailed error taxonomy used in TOBench analysis. The main
paper discusses the five top-level categories, while this appendix
enumerates the finer-grained subcategories used for trajectory
annotation and error heatmaps.

| Criterion Type |  What It Checks |  Typical Targets |  Typical Verification |
|----|----|----|----|
| Format Constraints |  Deterministic structural requirements explicitly specified by the task. |  File names, storage paths, worksheet names, schema fields, document sections, required output formats. |  Code-based checks over file existence, schema compliance, structural parsing, and exact field matching. |
| Judge-Based Multimodal Constraints |  Semantic or visual properties that cannot be robustly reduced to exact string matching. |  Layout fidelity, required visual evidence, semantic content consistency, object presence, rendered document quality under task-defined constraints. |  VLM-based judging after appropriate preprocessing such as rendering documents, parsing tables, or converting images to model-readable inputs. |
| Tool/Result Constraints |  Grounding requirements tied to tool usage or live external information rather than static reference files alone. |  Required MCP invocation, search-grounded facts, map or weather results, externally updated values, tool-derived fields in generated files. |  Tool-log verification and, when needed, re-querying external tools or MCP servers at evaluation time to validate grounded results. |

Table 5: Taxonomy of task-specific evaluation points in TOBench.
Different tasks mix these criterion types in different ways, which
motivates per-task evaluator synthesis rather than a single
benchmark-wide scoring template.

## Appendix E Extra Analysis for TOBench

### E.1 Multimodal Capability Deficit

#### E.1.1 Fine-grained Perception

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/wedding_layout_sketch.jpg)

Figure 7: Rough floor plan for the Johnson-Smith wedding
layout_sketch.jpg.

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/wedding_excel_gt.png)

(a)

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/wedding_excel_result.png)

(b)

Figure 8: Comparison of output results: (a) Ground truth for the
signature placement task; (b) Final image generated by Gemini 3 Pro.

In the task Customer_Service/Hotel_Wedding_Layout, agent (Gemini 3 Pro)
needs to count the types and quantities of tables and chairs required
for the wedding based on the wedding seating sketch provided by the
user. It shall then fill in the unit prices of seats specified in the
hotel’s domain rules into an Excel sheet, and use Excel formulas to
calculate the final results.
During the execution process, the agent successfully viewed the layout
sketch image but failed to accurately count the number of chairs to be
included in the budget. It wrote 28 chairs into the Excel file, whereas
the ground truth was 27.

#### E.1.2 Visual-Spatial Understanding

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/rental_agreement_input.jpg)

(a)

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/rental_agreement_result.png)

(b)

Figure 9: Initial and output files for the signature placement task: (a)
Original lease agreement image (rental_agreement.jpg); (b) Output
generated by Qwen 3.5 Plus showing spatial misalignment.

In the task Customer_Service/Real_Estate-rental_agreement, agent (Qwen
3.5 Plus) needs to use visual recognition to precisely locate the
signature labels and lines at the bottom of the agreement within the
source image. Subsequently, the agent must dynamically scale the
signature images based on the line length and transparently composite
them onto specific pixel coordinates while ensuring no contract text is
obstructed.
During the execution process, the agent continuously attempted to adjust
the placement and scaling of the images from turn 5 to turn 40. However,
the final results show that the landlord’s signature overlaps the text
labels, while the tenant’s signature severely deviates from the
designated area and even obscures the footer. Furthermore, the signature
dimensions are oversized, which directly violates domain rules regarding
proportional scaling and positional alignment.

In the task Customer_Service_TAN/Food_Delivery-delivery_problems_report,
the agent needs to first verify the courier’s identity by retrieving
data from an Excel order table based on the provided order number.
Subsequently, the agent is required to perform a frame-by-frame analysis
of the video evidence to objectively record violations such as food
damage or verbal conflicts, reconstruct the cause of the dispute (e.g.,
a tip-related confrontation), and ultimately generate a formal
investigation report titled incident_report.docx following a predefined
structure that includes penalty and compensation recommendations.
During the execution process, due to a fixed-frame extraction strategy
(every 10 seconds) and a lack of deep video causality modeling, the
agent (MiniMax M2.5) failed to capture or understand the continuous
actions of the courier within the temporal dimension. This led the agent
to completely miss critical aggressive behaviors, such as the deliberate
throwing of food and the confrontation over a tip, resulting in the
false conclusion that there was no evidence of aggressive behavior.

#### E.1.4 Cross-modal Information Fusion

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to caption](2605.16909v1/uber_gt.jpg)

Figure 10: Ground truth screenshot displaying the work hours record
interface.

In the task Customer_Service/Food_Delivery-ubereats_negative, the agent
needs to act as a multimodal content assistant by processing a video
clip, which first requires using speech recognition technology to
accurately extract and condense the author’s three core reasons for not
recommending work as an UberEats courier. These reasons must be
transformed into concise social media captions suitable for Instagram
and organized into a Word document titled
UberEats_Instagram_Content.docx. Simultaneously, the agent must
demonstrate cross-modal alignment capabilities by identifying and
capturing a data interface showing working hours or income statistics
from the video during the specific segment where the author discusses
the first reason, saving it as a standalone image file named
UberEats_WorkHours_Screenshot.png while strictly adhering to naming
conventions and file organization requirements.
During the execution process, Gemini 3.1 Pro successfully utilized an
audio_to_text tool to obtain the transcript and identify the starting
point of the first reason’s discussion; however, it exhibited
significant deficiencies in multimodal information fusion. Specifically,
the agent failed to effectively map the semantic timeline of the audio
to the visual timeline of the video, leading to a failure in the
keyframe capture request. Instead of extracting the statistical
interface from the beginning of the video, it erroneously captured a
frame at the 40-second mark showing an unrelated outdoor scene. This
failure in cross-modal alignment directly caused the task results to
deviate severely from the user’s requirements, exposing the model’s
insufficient depth in understanding complex audiovisual semantic
correlations.

#### E.1.5 Multimodal Hallucination

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In the task Intelligent_Creation/Game-bug_report, the agent needs to
precisely locate the trigger moment of a Minecraft item duplication
glitch by reviewing gameplay footage to identify the exact second
enchanted gear abnormally appears. The agent must then extract three PNG
keyframes representing the moments before, during, and after the trigger
and generate a standardized report titled
mc_item_duplication_bug_report.docx that includes precise MM:SS
timestamps, detailed reproduction steps, and an evidence attachment
list.
During the execution process, the GPT 4o exhibited severe hallucinations
by skipping the actual visual reasoning process after viewing only the
first frame of the video. Consequently, it fabricated the glitch trigger
moment and all subsequent reproduction steps and timestamp data, failing
to fulfill the domain rule of confirming the actual trigger time.
````
